walkthrough:
**What is a structural isomer?**

Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural formulae. For alkanes this means same number of carbons joined in a different order.

For alkanes: $$\text{general formula } C_nH_{2n+2}$$

**Find the formula of Q**

Count carbons in the skeletal formula. Every end of a line is a $\text{CH}_3$, every junction is a $\text{CH}_2$, $\text{CH}$ or $\text{C}$.

Q has a 9-carbon longest chain with 5 methyl branches:
$$\text{2,3,5,7,8-pentamethylnonane = } C_9 + 5 = C_{14}H_{30}$$

**Compare each option**

Count carbons the same way. Only a $C_{14}$ alkane can be an isomer. A $C_{14}$ alkane with exactly the same connectivity as Q is identical, not an isomer.

Counting gives B as $C_{12}$, D as $C_{13}$, A and C as $C_{14}$. A is the same 2,3,5,7,8-pattern as Q just flipped, while C is $C_{14}$ with a different branching pattern, so it is the structural isomer.

options.A: Has 14 carbons so same molecular formula as Q, but it is the same carbon skeleton as Q, just drawn with the right-hand end rotated. Identical molecules are not structural isomers.
options.B: Has a different total carbon count from Q, about C12, so its molecular formula is different, e.g. C12H26 versus C14H30. Different formula cannot be an isomer.
options.C: Has 14 carbons like Q so formula C14H30, but the branches are arranged in a different way with more branching around the centre. Same formula, different structure, so a true structural isomer.
options.D: Has only 13 carbons, one methyl branch missing compared to Q, so formula C13H28. Different molecular formula, so not an isomer.
